title: Task Tokens
one_liner: Instead of retuning the whole foundation model for each new robot task, train a tiny separate encoder that generates specialized tokens for the frozen model to read.
lead: Behavior foundation models are large pretrained robots that can follow many instructions at once. But for a specific task like opening a door, they often need careful prompt tweaking to work well. This paper introduces Task Tokens: keep the foundation model completely unchanged, and instead train a small separate encoder that learns to produce specialized tokens tailored to each task. The foundation model reads these task tokens and adjusts its behavior accordingly—like adding a thin lens on top of a good telescope instead of grinding a new telescope.

paras: Behavior foundation models are large pretrained systems that can output robot actions for many different tasks when you describe the task in the right way. A robot might follow walking commands, grasping commands, kicking commands—all from the same model.

The problem: for each new specific task, you either fiddle endlessly with the exact wording (prompt engineering), or you retrain the entire massive model (fine-tuning). Both are awkward. Prompt engineering wastes human time on trial and error. Fine-tuning retrains millions of parameters per task, which is slow and risks erasing what the model learned before.

callout.html: A foundation model can do many things, but it needs either tedious hand-tuning or expensive full retraining to do one specific thing well.

panels.title: 1. Foundation model receives a goal
panels.caption: A pretrained robot model knows how to reach, walk, kick from training on many behaviors.

panels.title: 2. Old way: prompt engineering
panels.viz_args: Try 'open door'. Nope. Try 'push door handle'. Better. Try 'use hand to push'. Much better.
panels.caption: Humans fiddle with wording until the robot does the right thing. Time-consuming and fragile.

panels.title: 3. Task Tokens: a learnable lens
panels.caption: A tiny separate encoder learns task-specific tokens. Foundation model stays frozen.

panels.title: 4. Encoder sees task, generates tokens
panels.viz_args: Task 'open door' + agent state -> Encoder -> Task tokens [0.3, -0.8, 1.2, ...]
panels.caption: The small encoder outputs 512 learned numbers tailored to the task, once per step.

panels.title: 5. Foundation model reads tokens and acts
panels.caption: Foundation model combines task tokens with regular goals. One model, many tasks.

steps.text: Encoder sees the goal (position, direction) and current robot state (joint angles, position).
Encoder runs through a small neural network, outputs 512 learned numbers tailored to this task.
Foundation model receives the task token plus the goal, generates next action.
Robot takes the action, measures success (did it move closer to the goal?).
Use reward signal to tweak the tiny encoder's parameters. Foundation model never changes.

paras: The paper introduces a new learnable object: a small encoder network (about 200,000 parameters) that generates task-specific tokens. This encoder sits between the task description and the frozen foundation model. Instead of either hand-tuning prompts or retraining the foundation model, you train only this tiny encoder to produce the right tokens for each task.

hidden.name: task token representation
paras: A task token is a list of 512 learned numbers produced by the encoder. Each number encodes one aspect of what the task requires. Unlike a hand-written prompt (which is human words), task tokens are learned numbers tuned by trial and error to make the foundation model behave correctly for the task.

The paper measures and optimizes these tokens by running the foundation model with them, collecting rewards (how well did the robot do?), and using reinforcement learning (where the model learns what direction nudges improve results, specifically PPO) to adjust the encoder toward generating better tokens.

heat.caption: Each cell is one learned number. Darker cells matter more for the task. Highlighted cells are critical for the behavior.

reads.html: A task token is just a learned list of numbers (512 of them) that tells the foundation model how to behave for this specific task.
Task tokens are learned numbers in the slot-space where the large model reads instructions, optimized by measuring reward to maximize task-specific goals.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the frozen model + learned tokens
paras: The foundation model is a large system that was trained on millions of real robot motions. It learned what good behaviors look like for many tasks. When you retrain the whole model, you risk overwriting that knowledge. Task Tokens avoids this by freezing the model completely.

Instead, a small encoder learns to speak the foundation model's language. The encoder produces tokens—numbers that fit into slots where the foundation model reads its instructions. When the foundation model reads these task-specific tokens alongside the goal, it automatically produces a behavior tailored to the task. Why? The foundation model already knows how to combine different signals (goals, state, tokens) because it was trained on many tasks. You only need to learn what specific numbers to produce for your new task.

Why is this better? The small encoder (200K parameters) trains fast because it has few numbers to adjust. Meanwhile, it draws on all the knowledge in the massive frozen foundation model (millions of parameters) that already knows how to act well. You get task specialization without expensive retraining.

stages.s: Task description plus current robot state
Foundation model (frozen) reads tokens and goal

math.words: Maximize the expected future reward by adjusting the encoder's parameters, while keeping the foundation model fixed.
math.equation: optimize_encoder: max E[sum_t gamma^t r_t] subject to BFM frozen
symbols: the tiny neural network you train
reward at step t (e.g., distance to goal decreased)
total expected reward over the episode

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Step 1: Encoder sees goal 'reach coordinate (1, 0)' and robot state 'at (0, 0)'. Encoder outputs token [0.5, -0.3, 0.8, ...].
Step 2: Foundation model reads token + goal, predicts action 'move arm forward'.
Step 3: Robot moves, distance to goal shrinks from 1.0 to 0.8. Reward r_1 = 0.2.
Step 4: Gradient flows back through frozen foundation model into encoder. Encoder learns: 'the tokens I made led to +0.2 reward, nudge that direction'.
Step 5: Repeat 50 million times. Encoder converges to tokens that maximize total reward.

math.note: The foundation model is a gradient highway—reward signals flow backward through it to update the encoder, but the model's own weights never change.

charts.title: Parameters per task
charts.note: Task Tokens needs 125x fewer parameters than full fine-tuning because it only trains a tiny encoder, not the whole model.

charts.title: Convergence speed
charts.note: Million training steps to reach the same performance. Fewer parameters mean fewer numbers to adjust, so training finishes sooner. Direct reward signals (measuring if the robot succeeded at the task) tell the encoder immediately what to fix, versus methods that retrain the whole model and blur which parameters matter.

items.html: Each task needs its own encoder and token set. If you want to handle 100 different tasks, you train 100 separate encoders. This trades task specialization for model count.

The encoder is a simple feedforward network in the paper. If you pick a bad architecture, it may not learn good tokens. Richer encoder designs (e.g., with more layers, or mechanisms that compare different parts of the input) could learn faster, because more structure gives the network more ways to combine the task information before producing tokens.

The encoder optimizes for rewards you hand-design. If the reward is wrong, the tokens will be wrong. You have not eliminated the need for good task specification—you have just moved it from prompt engineering to reward design.
Keep the reward simple and aligned with the true goal. Use the encoder to specialize the behavior, not to invent new task semantics.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train a task encoder for one new task (e.g., opening a door) using PPO. Freeze a behavior foundation model. Measure two things: (1) How many steps until the robot succeeds? (2) How many parameters did you train? Compare against prompt engineering (manual goal tweaking) and full fine-tuning (retraining the entire model).
demo.metric_eq: Success rate = (episodes where goal achieved) / (total episodes). Convergence speed = steps to 50% success. Parameters trained = encoder parameters only.
demo.closing: Task Tokens wins when: the encoder reaches 50% success in far fewer steps than fine-tuning, and with 100x fewer parameters. The foundation model never changed—all learning happened in the tiny encoder.
